summary: An announcement about the ARPA Network Control Center at BBN. It was now staffed 24 hours a day, every day, so users should call about IMP, TIP or network problems at any time. It gives a new phone number and asks sites to post it near their IMPs.

plainLanguage.summary: The helpdesk for the network is now open all day and night, and it has a new phone number. People are asked to stick it near their machines.

questions: who to call for arpanet problems
subtitle: Announcement that the ARPANET Network Control Center is now staffed 24/7 with a new phone number.

tldr.problem: Network operators had limited hours to report problems with the ARPANET's IMPs and TIPs, and the single phone number was often busy.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Control Center staff was expanded and scheduled to cover all hours, and a new phone number was published to reduce busy signals.
tldr.outcome: Sites could now reach network support at any time and had a dedicated number to post near their equipment.

today: RFC 356 is a historical operational notice from the early ARPANET. It documents the practical challenge of supporting a growing network and the importance of reliable communication channels between operational staff and sites.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 356 is a brief announcement from the ARPA Network Control Center at Bolt Beranek and Newman Inc. It informs the network community that the NCC has expanded its operational coverage and is now manned 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, so sites can report IMP and TIP problems at any time.
sections.plainLanguage: The network's help desk used to have limited hours. Now it is always open so people can get help any time, day or night.

sections.title: The New Phone Number
sections.content:
The RFC announces a new phone number for the NCC: (617) 661-0100. It explains that the old number had been getting busy signals, which this change is meant to fix. Sites are asked to post the new number prominently near their IMPs and inform their staff.

The RFC notes that the old number will continue to work for a while, but the new number should be preferred. It also asks that if anyone does get a busy signal, they should keep trying but also inform the operator when they connect so the NCC can track the problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Here is the new number to call: (617) 661-0100. Write it down and put it where everyone can see it. If you get a busy signal, keep calling but tell the person who answers that you got a busy signal.

sections.title: Contact and Coordination
sections.content: The RFC gives the mailing address for written communications to the NCC in Cambridge, Massachusetts. It also lists parties to be notified of changes or emergencies, including field service managers and contacts at sites without station agents, reflecting the distributed nature of the early ARPANET and the importance of coordination.
sections.plainLanguage: If you need to write to the help desk instead of calling, you can mail them a letter. The RFC also lists all the important people who need to know about network problems.
